objective: Test of the three steps (0.C scope, 0.GAP pre, 0.3 observe) on subgroup M21_asking, Asking, inquiring (#2316)
how: Read each verse in its passage with every finding in focus (RO1, RO2). Record findings in `findings` (observationrecord's shape: key, kind, text, meaning, implication, basis, route on a party or link finding, nodes [{verse, strong, surface, cluster, role}]; the surface names the occurrence; a description already live is named as existing and gains nodes). `words` lists only the surfaces of the verse (a surface is a word as written with its Strong) that lack what reading.surface_requirements asks, as `missing`: add only that. A surface lacking nothing is not listed (`surfaces_complete`). `open_items` are the open items for the verse, whatever their subgroup. A surface that cannot be completed takes its `record`: {"reason": ...}, {"item": "OT-nn.n|#n"} or {"new_item": <Open-Item add shape>}. A finding no longer supported: `withdraw` [{"node": id, "reason"} | {"observation": id, "reason"}]. The prompts are the catalogue's questions by kind: a prompt that does not apply is not answered (RG-17). Then Reading.ps1 -Step Record -Label m21-asking-test.

claims.text: Idols are taken "into their hearts" (Eze 14:3–7); the heart "goes after" idols (Eze 20:16); a "spirit of whoredom" leads astray (Hos 4:12) (dep §2.1i, §2.3c)

Most "spirit of …" phrases name a disposition that comes upon a person; the verse does not name a being. The same phrasing is used for good gifts: a spirit of wisdom, skill, grace, justice. Some are given by God: "the Lord has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep" (Isa 29:10); the harmful spirit "from the Lord" (1Sa 16:14); God "sent an evil spirit" (Judg 9:23); the Lord "put a lying spirit" in the prophets' mouths (1Ki 22:23). 2Ti 1:7 says "God gave us a spirit not of fear". Spirit-beings are real (unclean spirits cast out; the spirit of divination, Act 16:16), but the one-to-one mapping to vice families is not in the text (SC; dep §2.3c; D §11.4)
Each person answers for his own sin, and sin can be put away while a death still follows
One way the Old Testament speaks of where the dying go is going down to Sheol; it says where Sheol lies (beneath, the measure of depth) but not what it is made of
Scripture counts a life in days and says what the days are for
People sometimes want to die; of the 24 verses with such a wish, 17 name no inner word
Of the seven wishes to die answered in these passages, two are fed, two are answered another way, and three are granted, each to a man already blinded or wounded
Gentleness in meeting a wrong is joined to watching oneself, remembering what one was, and leaving the outcome to God
The offering is weighed by what is inside the one who brings it: an ear opened, the law in the heart, a broken heart, a love that lasts
Knowing that God's hand is on him is the named ground of Ezra's courage, and the courage turns at once into a deed
Those on whom God's good hand rests name it as the reason for what came about, and it is said to be for good on all who seek him
In the parable of the banquet the master's anger rests on the invited guests' refusals, turns into a wider invitation to the poor, and ends with the refusers shut out
Fear and anguish are shown in the body, and the verses see them first in the hands: hands fall at a report, grow feeble as the heart melts, and are held as in labour
Solomon on his throne showed honour upward to his mother, then refused her request
Anger can rise at contempt for a request that rested on good done
Adonijah's wish for Abishag was read by Solomon as the throne asked for again; the verses give Solomon's reading, not Adonijah's heart
A promise not to refuse can be overridden by an oath
When a people choose a king, their choosing and the Lord's setting of him are stated together; the choice binds loyalty, and a king chosen for themselves can meet no answer from the Lord.

findings_in_focus.text: In 1Kgs.22.8, 2Chr.18.7, Deut.13.14, and Deut.17.4 the sense of darash sits squarely within its base gloss of formal/careful inquiry (of the Lord, or of an alleged matter) with no notable divergence from the general stepGloss.

In Deut.13.14 the addressed Israelite (party, second-person singular) is commanded to initiate the inquiry, directed toward establishing the truth of a reported abomination -- an operation aimed at a matter/situation rather than a person.

In Deut.13.14 M13 (true/H0571H) and M23/M65 (certain) and M58 (abomination) co-occur; the inquiry (H1875) is the procedural means by which truth (M13) and certainty (M23) about the alleged abomination (M58) are to be established -- these M-codes describe the epistemic GOAL of the inquiry rather than a co-equal characteristic modifying it.

Since this subgroup's only member is H1875, there is no other member strong to compare it against within this pass; the cross-strong comparison task instead resolves to confirming internal coherence -- the 60 occurrences covered here (across 'Seek/inquire/inquired/require/searched/seeking') all sit within the single semantic family of deliberate, purposeful resort to a source of authority, verdict, or accountability (whether God, prophet, false deity, legal matter, or social/pastoral object of care), matching the subgroup definition of formal consultation and diligent inquiry with no genuinely divergent unrelated sense found in this batch.

The mechanism of seeking differs by context: toward God it operates through prayer/worship and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, 2Kgs.3.11 -- via a prophet); toward false gods it operates through idolatrous consultation or necromancy (1Sam.28.7, 2Kgs.1.2 -- via mediums); toward legal/moral matters it operates through investigation and testimony-checking (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18 -- via diligent inquiry and witnesses). The underlying mechanism shifts between mediated divine consultation, illicit occult consultation, and forensic investigation.

The mode of operation varies markedly by context: toward God it operates via prayer, worship, and prophetic mediation (1Kgs.22.8, Ps.77.2); toward idols/mediums it operates via necromancy and consultation of the dead (1Sam.28.7, Deut.18.11, Isa.8.19); in judicial contexts it operates via formal investigation and cross-examination of witnesses (Deut.13.14, 17.4, 19.18, Judg.6.29); and toward abstract objects (justice, welfare, a lost object) it operates as diligent practical pursuit (Isa.1.17, Deut.22.2). The constitutional level engaged also varies -- from whole-hearted devotion (soul/heart level) to procedural legal action (behavioral level).

passage.text: “ Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, ‘ Please let me drink.’
She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, ‘ Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.’ So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.
Then I asked her, ‘ Whose daughter are you?’ She said, ‘The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor’s son, whom Milcah bore to him.’ So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.

findings_in_focus.meaning: Meaning: fear of people stops speech (Joh 7:13), keeps a disciple secret (Joh 19:38), locks a door (Joh 20:19), and draws a man back from the table (Gal 2:12). Joh 9:22 states what was feared: being put out of the synagogue. Implies: Gal 2:13 names what followed as hypocrisy. At the locked door, the answer is a presence and a word ("Peace be with you"), and then "the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord" (Joh 20:20).

findings_in_focus.text: Fear leads to hiding, distance: "I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself"; "the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off"; "secretly for fear of the Jews"; "the doors being locked … for fear of the Jews"
Fear and Doubt and hiding (M20): Fear and hiding; "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"; a secret disciple (verses shared or near: 16 / 8).

Hiding from people: Much of the hiding in Scripture is from people who could do harm, and in these verses it is the weaker side that hides. "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). "The poor of the earth all hide themselves" (Job 24:4). When Israel hid in the caves, "all the people followed him trembling" (1 Samuel 13:7).; Often the verse records not the feeling of the one who hides but someone else's counsel to hide.; Jonathan: "Saul my father seeks to kill you … Stay in a secret place and hide yourself" (1 Samuel 19:2).; God to Elijah: "hide yourself by the brook Cherith" (1 Kings 17:3).; Where the feeling is named, it is fear.; Jacob fled from Laban "secretly", and he said why: "Because I was afraid" (Genesis 31:27, 31).; Joseph of Arimathea was "a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews". The same verse ends with him going to Pilate and taking away the body (John 19:38).; Hiding can be good sense: "The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it" (Proverbs 22:3). It ends when the news changes. The men who had hidden in the hills "heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle" (1 Samuel 14:22).; And sometimes hiding is refused, or impossible.; The servant chooses not to hide: "I gave my back to those who strike … I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6).; No one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend" (Psalm 55:12–13).

Where inner being is present, it sits behind the act (phenomenon.set hidden-behind-act), and the motive is named by *another cluster's* word: fear: Gen 3:10 ("I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself"); Mat 25:25 ("I was afraid, and I went and hid your talent"); Joh 19:38 ("secretly for fear of the Jews"); Dan 10:7 ("a great trembling fell upon them, and they fled to hide themselves"); 1Ch 21:20 (Ornan's sons hid on seeing the angel); shame or withdrawal: Luk 1:24, Elizabeth "kept herself hidden". The motive follows in 1:25: "to take away my reproach among people".; Hiding is the body's answer to fear. The seat is replaced by the act together with the fear word.
How it co-exists across the strands. Trembling (1Sa 13:7; Dan 10:7), fear (Gen 31:31; Joh 19:38), and seeing danger (Pro 22:3; 1Ch 21:20). Its opposite is the prudent/simple pair (f).

As a standing toward God: commanded, learned, given: "what does the Lord your God require of you, but to fear the Lord your God"; "that they may hear and learn to fear the Lord your God"; "I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me"
Face D. Fearing God as a standing (177 / 170 hits and verses, units 1–4): Commanded, learned, given, owed, lived
Fear and Worship and service (M36): Commanded together: "to fear the Lord your God … to serve the Lord" (verses shared or near: 56 / 24).
Fear and Love (M51): Commanded together (fear, walk, love, serve); set against ("perfect love casts out fear") (verses shared or near: 10 / 5).

0. Data notes: "whatever my eyes desired [*asked*]" (Ecc 2:10); "what does the Lord your God require [*ask*] of you" (Deu 10:12); It is read in §2. It overlaps with M42 petition; no ruling is raised.; Lexical notes carried into the analysis: *bārak* "bless" as a euphemism for "curse" (Job 1:5; 2:5; Psa 10:3) [lexical]; *rāṣâ* "accept" = "pay off" (Lev 26:41, 43 "make amends"; Isa 40:2 "her iniquity is pardoned"); *kāvôd* "glory" = the self (§3.2); *gōʾēl* "redeemer" = "avenger of blood" (§11.1); G3670 "confess" has two active rows: T3 (LLM · low · review_flag) and M60 (escalation 1714, high). This is a DB note only.; 1Jo 5:7 has a G4151G row with no surface form and class n/a ("For there are three that testify:"). The ESV text has no "Spirit" in this verse; the next verse (1Jo 5:8) begins "the Spirit and the water and the blood". This is a tagging artefact [verify]. It is noted and not used.; "Speak to the heart" is an idiom [lexical]. *dibbēr ʿal-lēv* = speak kindly / tenderly / encouragingly: Gen 34:3; 50:21; Judg 19:3; Rut 2:13; 2Sa 19:7; Hos 2:14; Isa 40:2; 2Ch 30:22; 32:6. The surface shows "kindly / tenderly", and the M47 tag sits on it. It is kept in §1.4, because it shows the heart as the addressee of speech.; Distance note. Positions are in original-language word order [verify]. d0 occurs at Rom 12:1 "spiritual worship" and at Hos 4:8 / Jer 22:27, where *nāśāʾ nephesh* is one idiom.
What God asks: "what does the Lord your God require [*ask*] of you, but … to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deu 10:12).

4.1 Serving with all the heart and all the soul: "to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul" (Deu 10:12; 11:13; Jos 22:5); "serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind [*soul*], for the Lord searches all hearts" (1Ch 28:9); "serve him faithfully with all your heart" (1Sa 12:24; 12:20); "direct your heart to the Lord and serve him only" (1Sa 7:3)

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

3.2 Totality and wholeness formulas: *Heart and soul (and might):*; "with all your heart and with all your soul (and with all your might)" (Deu 4:29; 6:5; 10:12; 11:13; 13:3; 26:16; 30:2, 6, 10; Jos 22:5; 1Ki 2:4; 8:48; 2Ki 23:3, 25; 2Ch 6:38; 15:12; 34:31; Jer 32:41 — said of God); "you know in your hearts and souls" (Jos 23:14); "lay up these words … in your heart and in your soul" (Deu 11:18); "keep your soul diligently, lest … they depart from your heart" (Deu 4:9); "I am with you heart and soul" (1Sa 14:7, ESV idiom; only *lēvāv* is tagged); "one heart and soul" (Act 4:32); *NT expansion — heart, soul, mind, strength:* Mat 22:37; Mar 12:30; Luk 10:27; "heart … understanding … strength" (Mar 12:33).; *Whole person with an outer term added:*; "spirit and soul and body" (1Th 5:23); "soul and body" (Isa 10:18; Mat 10:28; Psa 31:9; Pro 16:24); "heart and flesh" (Psa 73:26; 84:2; Eze 44:7, 9); "body and spirit" (1Co 7:34; 2Co 7:1); "vexation from your heart … pain from your body" (Ecc 11:10); [Claude reading] Wholeness is expressed by *adding* terms, not by defining parts. The pairs work as merisms: the whole person seen from two or three sides at once.

findings_in_focus.text: Turned onto what is feared, the root describes: God himself, "the great, the mighty, and the awesome God" (Deu 10:17; 7:21), the great and awesome God "who keeps covenant and steadfast love" in three prayers (Neh 1:5; 9:32; Dan 9:4); his name (Psa 99:3; 111:9; Deu 28:58); his deeds (Psa 66:3, 5; 145:6; 106:22; Exo 34:10; Isa 64:3); his day, "great and very awesome; who can endure it?" (Joe 2:11, 31; Mal 4:5); a place (Gen 28:17); an angel's appearance (Jdg 13:6); the wilderness, "great and terrifying" (Deu 1:19; 8:15); an invading nation, "dreaded and fearsome" (Hab 1:7); a people "feared near and far" (Isa 18:2, 7); the living creatures' rims and the crystal expanse (Eze 1:18, 22); the human frame, "I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:14).

findings_in_focus.text: Want (M18) is the root motivating content behind the asking (M21) which is executed in haste (M67) -- want causes/drives the whole sequence, same party (the girl), same target (the king).

G4710 is exclusively nominal across all twelve of its occurrences (N-ASF, N-GSF, N-DSF forms), meaning the subgroup's noun-member consistently names diligence/zeal/haste as a possessable, giveable, or measurable quality (something one 'shows', 'has produced in you', 'puts into a heart', or is measured 'by') -- structurally opposite to G4709's pure manner-of-action adverbial function. This is the clearest grammatical-role divergence between the two subgroup members: G4710 names the THING, G4709 describes the HOW.

G4710's occurrence list shows a wider register-range than G4709's: it covers pure physical haste with no moral overtone (Mark 6:25, Herodias's daughter rushing to the king with a grim request; Luke 1:39, Mary's journey), alongside heavily moralized/evidentiary senses in the Pauline corpus (2Cor 7:11-12, 8:7-8; used as proof of sincerity of repentance or love) and paired-virtue senses (Rom 12:8, 12:11; Heb 6:11; 2Pet 1:5, chained with faith/virtue/knowledge). G4709's three occurrences, by contrast, are uniformly positive/earnest in register (pleading, searching, doing one's best) with no neutral-or-negative-context instance comparable to Mark 6:25's use for a request tied to John the Baptist's beheading -- showing G4710 tolerates a broader range of surrounding moral valence than G4709 does within this subgroup.

Varied. The immediate response ranges from urgent physical motion (Mark 6:25's rush to the king; Luke 1:39's haste to the hill country) to an urgent verbal appeal (Luke 7:4's earnest pleading) to an inward resolve to write (Jude 1:3) -- the register of the immediate response shifts by context though the urgency itself is constant.

Varies by context. In narrative contexts (Mark 6:25, Luke 1:39, Luke 7:4) the felt quality is transient urgency tied to a specific occasion. In hortatory/epistolary contexts (Rom 12:11, Heb 6:11, 2Pet 1:5) it is framed as a settled disposition to be maintained or grown into over time.

In Mark 6:25 the haste accompanies a speech-act (the daughter's request, 'saying, I want you to give me...') and in Jude 1:3 the eagerness modifies the intent to write -- both show the characteristic bound up with a communicative act, though the characteristic itself is the manner of approach/desire to speak rather than the speech content.

The pattern of occurrence shows the characteristic seated primarily at the level of will/spirit engaged in directed action, paired explicitly with 'spirit' in Rom 12:11 ('fervent in spirit') and with 'heart' in 2Cor 8:16 (placed 'into the heart of Titus'). It never engages purely bodily/sensory levels in isolation, though physical motion (haste, Mark 6:25; Luke 1:39) is its outward expression. The heart/spirit link here is expressive -- the inner earnestness expresses itself outwardly through bodily action (hurrying) or verbal/practical deeds (pleading, providing), rather than the body generating the earnestness itself.

The characteristic ends where mere physical speed without moral/relational engagement occurs (Mark 6:25's haste tied to a grim, morally neutral-to-negative request shows the term can denote sheer speed without ethical earnestness) -- it is not synonymous with recklessness or hurried carelessness, nor with love or faith themselves, which it accompanies as evidence (2Cor 8:7-8) but does not constitute.
Whole network: want (M18) is the originating volitional core, expressed through asking (M21) and carried with haste (M67) -- want's role is the root cause driving the whole chain.
The operation 'give' (role-T3, which want governs as content) is initiated by the girl's demand and directed toward the king, who is asked to give the head at once.

Haste names the manner of the girl's entrance to the king; its role is to intensify urgency in delivering her mother's demand, marking her as fully compliant and eager to press it through immediately.
The haste is generated within the girl herself as she acts on her mother's instigation, an immediate self-driven urgency rather than bestowed or received from elsewhere.

This occurrence matches the term's usual 'haste/speed' sense (as also in Luke 1:39), showing no divergence from its typical usage; the surface form meta spoudes is the standard idiom for 'with haste.'
The immediate response shown is urgent resolve -- the girl moves at once to press her request without delay or hesitation.
No lasting inner quality or capacity is established by this single act of haste; it is a momentary manner of action in this scene.
No change in the girl's condition or disposition is shown; haste describes the manner of an already-decided action, not a transformation.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is depicted; haste marks the manner of a single continuous action.
No mechanism producing change is shown; haste is the manner in which the already-formed demand is carried out.
Haste operates as the manner-mode of urgent, immediate action -- entering and asking without delay.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for haste in this verse; it describes outward manner of action.
Haste here engages volition and agency -- it reflects the girl's determined, urgent will acting swiftly on her mother's instigation to press the demand.
Haste here is not movement toward God -- it describes urgent approach to a human king to demand an execution, not seeking, supplication, or worship of God.
Haste is the girl's own manner of action, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Haste is extended in the girl's approach toward the king -- she brings her mother's demand to him with urgent immediacy, operating as the pressing manner of that interpersonal request.
Haste is not depicted as taken up by the girl from another party here; it is her own manner in carrying out the demand (following her mother's instigation, but the haste itself is her own action).
No relation to angelic or adversarial beings is shown.
Haste is not predicated of God here; it describes purely human urgency in the girl's approach to Herod to demand John's execution.
Asked (αἰτέω) names the girl's formal request to the king; its role/effect is to convert her mother's instigation into a direct, binding demand upon Herod.
The immediate response shown is decisive, urgent demand -- the girl moves straight to stating exactly what she wants, without hesitation.
No lasting inner state or capacity is produced by this single request; it is a momentary act within the narrative.
No change in the girl's own condition or disposition is shown; she acts to secure an external outcome from the king.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is shown; the asking is a single decisive act.
No mechanism of inner change is shown; asking here is the immediate execution of the already-formed demand from want (M18).
Asking operates as a direct, spoken demand mode -- verbally stating exactly what is wanted to the one with power to grant it.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for this asking in the verse.
The asking originates within the girl herself as she acts on the wish (M18) instigated by her mother -- self-generated in the moment, though the underlying motive was received from another.
Asking here engages volition and agency -- the girl exercises her will directly, actively demanding rather than merely wishing.
This asking is directed at a human king, not toward God; it is not an act of seeking, supplication, or worship of God.
Asking here is the girl's own act toward the king, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Asking is extended by the girl toward the king -- it operates as a direct interpersonal demand pressed upon him for an immediate act (John's head).
Asking is not depicted as something the girl takes up from another; rather she carries her mother's instigated wish forward as her own request to the king.
No angelic or adversarial being is in view; the asking is directed at the human king Herod.
This asking is not predicated of God nor related to God; it is a purely human demand made to King Herod.
Want (θέλω) names the girl's stated desire; its role is to declare the specific outcome she is demanding -- John's head on a platter.
The immediate expression shown is a blunt, specific declaration of the desired outcome -- 'I want... at once' -- reflecting resolute will with no hesitation.
No lasting inner quality or capacity is produced by this single expressed want; it is a momentary declaration within the scene.
No change in the girl's own condition or disposition is shown; she expresses an already-fixed desire, not a transformation.
No before/during/after sequence of inner states is shown; want is voiced as a single fixed declaration.
The mechanism producing this want is the mother's instigation -- the desire was formed through another's influence and is here voiced by the girl as her own.
Want operates in the mode of direct volitional declaration -- stating the desired outcome plainly and pressing for its immediate fulfillment.
No specific constitutional level (spirit/soul/heart/mind/body part) is named for want in this verse.
The want is received from another person -- the girl's mother instigated the request, which the girl voices as her own desire to the king.
Want engages the volitional faculty directly -- it is the girl's own will expressed and pressed as demand upon the king.
This want is directed at a human king for a violent request, not movement toward God in seeking or worship.
Want here is the girl's own desire directed at the king, not an act proceeding from God toward a human person.
Want is extended by the girl toward the king as the content of her demand -- it operates as the interpersonal expression of what she requires of him.
The want the girl voices is taken up from her mother's instigation (implied by the wider narrative) -- she adopts and voices as her own the desire her mother directed her to express.
No angelic or adversarial being is involved; the want is directed at the human king Herod.
This want is not predicated of God nor related to God; it is a human desire voiced to a human king.
'In' (came in) is a plain movement-verb describing entrance, a supporting operation-word.
'Immediately' is a manner adverb intensifying the speed of the entrance; it modifies the operation rather than naming its own characteristic.
'With' is a preposition linking 'haste' to the action; it carries no independent characteristic.
'To' is a preposition marking direction toward the king; it names no characteristic of its own.
'King' names Herod's office/role; it is a supporting referential noun, not its own inner-being characteristic.
'Saying' introduces the girl's direct speech; it is a supporting speech-act verb, not its own characteristic.
'Give' is the plain operation-verb demanded of the king, a supporting act-word not its own characteristic.
'Me' is a plain first-person pronoun, the recipient of the demanded act; it names no characteristic of its own.
'Once' (at once) is a manner adverb intensifying the immediacy demanded; it qualifies the operation rather than naming its own characteristic.
'Head' names the literal body part demanded; it is a supporting concrete noun, not an inner-being characteristic.
'John' is a proper name identifying John the Baptist; it carries no meaningful inner-being sense to analyse.
'Baptist' is a title/epithet identifying John; it carries no independent inner-being characteristic to analyse here.
'On' is a preposition marking placement upon the platter; it carries no independent characteristic.
'Platter' names the literal serving dish demanded; it is a supporting concrete noun, not an inner-being characteristic.

As a genitive noun (N-GSF) inside the phrase 'with haste,' this occurrence's form shows spoude (haste) functioning as the manner of Herodias's daughter's entry, naming the urgency driving her approach to the king.
In the fixed phrase meta spoudes (with haste), this occurrence means literal physical speed/urgency of movement, the girl's rushing entrance to make her request, not zeal or diligence.

Here spoude marks the abruptness with which the request follows the mother's instruction, implying a constitutional urgency that colors the demand for John's head as impulsive rather than deliberated.
Rooted in speudo (to hasten), the term here operates as literal speed of physical movement into the king's presence, showing bodily urgency rather than inner earnestness.
As a genitive singular feminine noun governed by the preposition meta ('with'), the form functions adverbially, describing the manner of her coming in rather than naming an independent quality.

This occurrence sits at the 'haste/speed' end of the term's semantic range (as opposed to its 'zeal/earnestness' extension seen elsewhere, e.g. Rom.12.11), showing the physical rather than dispositional sense operating here.
This occurrence expresses an act (the manner of her hurried coming) rather than a settled disposition or received quality.
No related term functioning as this occurrence's structural opposite (e.g. a term for delay/sloth) is present in this verse's context.
No person-type term (one habitually characterized by haste) is relevant to or present in this occurrence.
No supplication/seeking term for obtaining haste from another applies to this occurrence.
As NT Greek narrative prose describing a court scene, the Testament context makes no special interpretive difference here beyond the ordinary Koine sense of hastening.
Spoude is attested in classical Greek (e.g. Herodotus, Thucydides) well before the NT period; this occurrence uses the term's established pre-NT sense of haste/speed, not a NT-period coinage.
The middle-voice aorist form (V-AMI-3S) shows the girl asking on her own behalf/for her own benefit, consistent with the middle sense of aiteo as claiming or requesting something for oneself.
Here aiteo means to ask/request of a superior (the king), functioning at the definitional level as a formal demand made to one with power to grant it.
The relational implication here is directional: the asking moves from an inferior party (the girl) to a superior (the king), carrying an expectation that he will grant it.
The root sense of aiteo, 'to ask/request,' operates here as a direct verbal petition put to the king for a specific object (the head on a platter).
As an aorist middle indicative verb, the form shows a completed, self-interested act of requesting, framing her question as a decisive single act rather than an ongoing plea.

This occurrence sits within the term's ordinary 'ask a person for a thing' range (accusative person + thing), not its logical/postulate or borrowing extensions, showing a straightforward request-of-a-superior sense.
This occurrence expresses an act (the specific act of requesting) rather than a disposition.
No related term functioning as a structural opposite (e.g. a term for refusing/withholding) is present in this occurrence's context.
No person-type term (one who habitually asks/petitions) is relevant to this occurrence.
Aiteo itself is the term's own supplication/seeking-from-another sense; here it directly names the act of the girl seeking the head from the king.
As NT Greek narrative describing a request to Herod, Testament context makes no special interpretive difference beyond ordinary Koine usage of asking a superior for something.
Aiteo is well attested in classical Greek from Homer onward; this occurrence uses its established pre-NT sense of asking/demanding, not a NT-period coinage.
This occurrence matches the term's usual 'ask/request of a superior' sense; no divergence from the ordinary usage is shown here.
The present active indicative first-person form (V-PAI-1S) shows the girl expressing her own immediate, ongoing will directly to the king, naming a present act of willing rather than a settled trait.
Here thelo means 'I wish/want,' functioning definitionally as a direct statement of personal desire preceding and driving the specific request that follows.

The implication here is constitutional: the girl asserts her own will as the driving force behind the demand, framing the request as an expression of what she herself wants rather than a mere relay of her mother's instruction.
The root sense of thelo, an act of will/wish, operates here as the stated motive introducing her specific demand ('I want you to give me... the head').

As a present active first-person singular verb followed by an infinitive/subjunctive construction, the form shows a direct, present-tense assertion of personal will governing the following clause of what should be given.

This occurrence sits within the term's core volitional range ('to will, wish, want'), specifically the sense of a firm intention/decision (cf. Lk 14:28) rather than mere inclination, matching her decisive framing of the demand.
This occurrence expresses an act of willing/wanting in the moment, rather than a fixed disposition.
No related term functioning as a structural opposite (e.g. a term for reluctance/refusal) is present in this occurrence's context.
No person-type term (one who habitually wills/desires) is relevant to this occurrence.

No separate supplication/seeking term is relevant here; the wanting itself is expressed directly by thelo, with the actual seeking-from-another carried by the neighboring verb aiteo, not by this term.
As NT Greek narrative dialogue, the Testament context makes no special interpretive difference here beyond ordinary Koine usage of thelo as 'want/wish.'
Thelo/ethelo is attested in classical Greek from Homer onward; this occurrence uses its established pre-NT sense of wishing/wanting, not a NT-period coinage.
This occurrence matches the term's usual 'wish/want' sense as a stated personal desire; no divergence from the ordinary usage is shown here.

(b) Demanding or giving full disclosure between persons.; Samuel "was afraid to tell the vision to Eli" (1Sa 3:15). Eli binds him with an oath, "Do not hide it from me" (3:17). "Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, 'It is the Lord. Let him do what seems good to him'" (3:18). And why should my father hide this from me?" (1Sa 20:2). This is trust in a father's openness, and chapter 20 proves it misplaced.; Kings demanding it: "Do not hide from me anything I ask you" (2Sa 14:18); "I will ask you a question; hide nothing from me" (Jer 38:14).; Under threat: "hide nothing from us and we will not put you to death" (Jer 38:25).; Disclosure of utter need: "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent … nothing left … but our bodies and our land" (Gen 47:18).

Seat.; In the verse, the bearer's own (genuine): Psa 40:10 "I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart". Batch A v3 §6 ("The heart can conceal or not"). The heart is the place where a word could be kept back, and the verse says it was not.; In the verse, the offender's own self: Isa 3:9 "they have brought evil on themselves [*their nephesh*]". Batch D v2 §2.3 ("Evil against one's own soul"). Seat-sense: *nephesh* is here the self, reflexively, and it passes the check in that sense. New in v3: the verse holds the phenomenon and its outcome together. The face does *not* conceal ("they do not hide it"), and the evil disclosed comes back on the self that disclosed it. Shamelessness is not a safe disclosure.; In the next verse, the other party's (genuine): Num 5:13 → 5:14 "the spirit of jealousy comes over him". The deed is hidden in the wife; the seat that registers it is the husband's spirit (v2).; A seat outside M47: Job 31:33 *chob*, "bosom", where the iniquity would be hidden (v1 §3 item 6; not an M47 word).; In the passage, the bearer's own — new in v3: Job 6:10 ("This would be my comfort … for I have not denied the words of the Holy One") is flanked by two uses of *nephesh*: "My appetite refuses to touch them; they are as food that is loathsome to me" (6:7). *Nephesh* is appetite here. The sense passes the check only as bodily desire, and it has turned to loathing.; "What is my strength, that I should wait? And what is my end, that I should be patient?" (6:11). *Nephesh* is inside the English "be patient", literally "lengthen my soul". It is genuine, and the soul cannot endure.; Job's one comfort, that he has not concealed God's words, stands between an appetite that loathes and a soul that can no longer wait. Not concealing is the one thing left intact.; Spurious context link: 2Sa 14:18 → 14:19 "As surely as you live [*nephesh*]" is an oath formula. Batch G v3 §4 read the formula as "the soul as what one swears by". It says nothing of the disclosure.; Whose seat, strand (b) and (e): none. The disclosures of Samuel, the kings' demands, the treasure-finder's joy and the servant's fear are all carried by speech and act, not by a seat word.

Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened": Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers: *"By no means!"* (v1). *"God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew"* (v2). He gives Elijah, who thought he was alone, and God's reply: *"I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal"* (v4). *"So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works"* (v5–6).; Then v7: *"What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"*.; The others are *"the rest"*. Two things are said of them: They were seeking (*epizēteō*, G1934) and did not obtain.; They were hardened (*pōroō*, G4456).; The hardening is described from Scripture: *"God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day"* (v8). The giving is God's act (rule 72, A). The eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear are in the human inner being.; Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

What this verse shows of others around the choosing: Those who are not among the chosen are described as seeking and not obtaining.; They were hardened: eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear (v8).; The hardening is not the end. Their stumbling is not *"in order that they might fall"* (v11).; Jealousy is named as an aim: *"so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11).; The remnant is chosen *"by grace"*, not by works (v5–6). The verse says how the elect were chosen. It does not say why the rest were not.

1 Thessalonians 1:4: "For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you": Paul writes of what he remembers of them: *"your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ"* (v3). Then: *"For we know, brothers loved by God, that he has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (v4–5).; "Know" is *oida* (G6063). Here another person knows that someone has been chosen. The ESV joins v4 to v5 with "because": the knowing rests on how the gospel came to them. The passage goes on to what was seen in them: *"you received the word in much affliction, with the joy of the Holy Spirit"* (v6); *"you became an example to all the believers"* (v7); *"your faith in God has gone forth everywhere"* (v8); *"you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven"* (v9–10)

Jesus answers twice with the will: *"If you would enter life, keep the commandments"* (19:17); *"If you would be perfect, go, sell … and come, follow me"* (19:21); He has kept the commandments and still asks, *"What do I still lack?"* (19:20). When the will is asked for the thing he holds, he *"went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions"* (19:22).; Probes: The will, the possessions and the feeling are named in one verse. That fits Rom 9:16, already in 10.7: "not on human will".

findings_in_focus.text: In John.16.19 zeteo shifts toward the sense 'inquire/discuss/question among yourselves' (the disciples questioning each other about the meaning of Jesus's saying), aligning with the tree's documented sense 'to inquire or ask questions' rather than physical search -- a cognitive/interpretive nuance distinct from the searching-for-a-person sense used elsewhere in John.

M15 (knew/ginosko, Jesus's knowledge) and M18 (wanted/thelo, the disciples' desire) co-occur with M83 seeking in John.16.19: Jesus's perceptive knowledge (M15) discerns the disciples' desire (M18) to ask, which surfaces as their mutual questioning (M83/zeteo). The seeking here is the visible symptom of the underlying want that Jesus's knowledge already perceives -- an epistemic chain (knowledge -> desire -> inquiry) rather than seeking acting on the others.

In John.16.19 the seeking/inquiring operation is initiated by the disciples (party, T8 via Jesus's interlocutors) directed toward one another ('among yourselves') and ultimately toward understanding Jesus's own saying.
In John.16.19 erotao is used in its plain interrogative sense 'to ask/question' Jesus about the meaning of his saying -- sitting within the base gloss with no notable divergence.

they were troubled → "Why are your faces downcast?" → "We have had dreams" (Gen 40:6–8).

What it does: It wears down over time: "her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her … So it went on year by year" (1Sa 1:6–7); It stops eating and brings weeping: "Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat" (1:7); It dims the eye and wastes the body: "My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow" (Job 17:7); It cannot be weighed: "Oh that my vexation were weighed … it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words have been rash" (Job 6:2–3); It shows in the face: Joseph "saw that they were troubled", and asks "Why are your faces downcast today?" (Gen 40:6–7).

findings_in_focus.text: Sequence in 1Sa 1:6–18: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.

What turns or settles a person's anger: soft answer → wrath turned (Pro 15:1); good sense → slow to anger (Pro 19:11); Aaron's answer → Moses heard → approved (Lev 10:16–20); servants' question → dipped → flesh restored (2Ki 5:13–14); poured out her soul, "Go in peace" → ate, face no longer sad (1Sa 1:15–18); sold me → angry with yourselves → do not, for God sent me (Gen 45:5); remember your brother has something against you → first be reconciled (Mat 5:23–24).
U1 §37, 1Sa 1:6–18: the reading says bitter of soul; the ESV says "She was deeply distressed" (1Sa 1:10); the text carries H5315I nep̄eš (soul), rendered "distressed", tagged M47.
provoked year by year → wept, would not eat (1Sa 1:7); poured out her soul, "Go in peace" → ate, face no longer sad (1:15–18).

What it leads to: Resolution through a word given: Eli's "Go in peace", and then "the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad" (1Sa 1:17–18). The body's signs reverse: she eats, and her face changes; Or a plea to be allowed to die: "that it would please God to crush me, that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!" (Job 6:9); Or interpretation: Joseph's "Please tell them to me" (Gen 40:8).

1Sa 1:6–18: Sequence the text gives: provoked year by year → weeping, not eating → heart named by husband → "deeply distressed" (Hebrew bitter of soul) → heart-prayer, lips only → misread as drunk → self-explanation ("vexation") → blessing → eats, face no longer sad.

Inner speech unheard by people: "Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard" (1Sa 1:13); Revisit 2026-09-28 (context 1Sa 1:7–18, Batch G §8.2): Before: she weeps and will not eat; "why is your heart sad?" (7–8). The prayer comes "after they had eaten and drunk" (9).; After: Eli takes her for drunk (14). She answers in exact inner vocabulary: "a woman troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul before the Lord" (15). Then "Go in peace", and "her face was no longer sad" (17–18).; [Claude reading] Unheard heart-speech is misread by a human hearer as drunkenness, the merry-heart state (Batch F §7), and is heard by God. It is the sad-heart counter-case to the merry heart at a feast.

What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: "let my soul die" (30); The merry-heart threshold is the penultimate step (G §3.6).; The counter-case: the sad heart at a feast.; Hannah "would not eat … why is your heart sad?" → prays "after they had eaten and drunk" → is taken for drunk → "troubled in spirit … pouring out my soul" → face no longer sad (1Sa 1:7–18).; Nehemiah: "when wine was before him … Why is your face sad? … sadness of the heart" → prayer → request granted (Neh 2:1–5).; The sad heart at the feast is also a threshold, but what enters is prayer, and the outcome is a gift (G §8.2).; Revisit (Batch H §7.6) — the threshold pattern extended again: Esther's wine-banquets (Est 5:6–14; 7:3–8): "as they were drinking wine after the feast" (5:6) → Haman goes out "joyful and glad of heart" (5:9) → sees Mordecai → wrath → "all this is worth nothing to me" (5:13) → the gallows (5:14).; At the second banquet Esther asks for her life (7:3). The king "arose in his wrath from the wine-drinking" (7:7), and Haman begs for his life (7:7–8).; One banquet is the threshold for two outcomes: Esther's petition is granted; Haman falls.; The threshold refused at the heart: "Daniel resolved [*set on his heart*] that he would not defile himself with the king's food, or with the wine that he drank" (Dan 1:8) → "fatter in flesh" than those who ate it (1:15). Compare Uriah (point 5).; The inner sentence comes first: "if that servant says to himself, 'My master is delayed,' and begins … to eat and drink and get drunk" → the master comes "on a day when he does not expect him" (Luk 12:45–46; Mat 24:48–51).; The warning: "watch yourselves lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness" (Luk 21:34).; The counter-statement: "the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" (Rom 14:17).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16) — the threshold and death: Nabal's sequel: the heart dies in the morning (1Sa 25:37), and "about ten days later the Lord struck Nabal, and he died" (25:38). The dead heart comes before the dead man.

verses.text: So they inquired again of the Lord, “Is there a man still to come?” and the Lord said, “ Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”

passage.text: Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot.
He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found.
So they inquired again of the Lord, “Is there a man still to come?” and the Lord said, “ Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward.
And Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see him whom the Lord has chosen? There is none like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”

And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.
At Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, “ Ask what I shall give you.”

And Solomon said, “ You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day.

passage.text: Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?”

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, “It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers.”
And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, “ Arise and eat.”
And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again.

findings_in_focus.text: Revisit (delta) — Elijah under the broom tree (context 1Ki 19:1–8): Jezebel: "if I do not make your life as the life of one of them" (2); "he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life" (3); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers'" (4); "he lay down and slept … an angel touched him and said, 'Arise and eat'" (5); A cake and a jar of water; "he ate and drank and lay down again" (6); "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you" (7); "he went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb" (8); [Claude reading]; He runs to save his life, then asks for it to be taken. Fear for the life and weariness of the life follow each other within a day.; The death-wish is answered with food, not with argument. The questions come later, at Horeb ("What are you doing here?", 19:9).; This is the eating-and-drinking threshold of Batch F §7, reversed. There, the meal lowers the guard and something enters. Here, the meal answers an exhausted soul and becomes strength ("the strength of that food"). Compare "strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread" (Judg 19:5; §3.1).; Four death-wishes, four answers (see §16.2 for the full set): Elijah (food), Jonah (a question about pity), Samson (granted, with strength), Saul (granted by another's hand, who then dies for it).
Elijah | "he asked that he might die … take away my life" (1Ki 19:4) | a threat to his life; flight (19:2–3) | Food from an angel, twice → strength for forty days (19:5–8) (§6)
Batch C v3 (delta) | "Life 'better' gone" (Jon 4:3, 8; 1Ki 19:4) | The before and after of these wishes are read in G §6 and §16.2. C's desire-reading stands | No change

The soul asks to die [lexical]: "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*] … 'take away my life'" (1Ki 19:4 — Elijah); "he asked that he might die [*asked his nephesh to die*]" (Jon 4:8 — Jonah), with "a scorching east wind" [*wind*]; [Claude reading] Two prophets, the same idiom: the self asks its own soul to die.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.

The human soul's revulsion at food, before death: "we loathe this worthless food" (Num 21:5); "they loathed any kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death" (Psa 107:18); "his life loathes bread" (Job 33:20).; Revisit (Batch G v3 §16.2): each of these is followed by a turn: Num 21: serpents → "when he sees it, shall live" (21:8–9); Psa 107: "they cried to the Lord … He sent out his word and healed them" (107:19–20); Job 33: a mediator's ransom → "let his flesh become fresh" (33:24–25); Set beside them, Elijah's death-wish is answered with food (1Ki 19:4–8).

What the pattern shows [Claude reading]: The threshold entered with death in view: the Lord "called for weeping and mourning … and behold, joy and gladness … eating flesh and drinking wine. 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'" → "this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (Isa 22:12–14). The feast is held against a call to mourn.; The threshold reversed: Elijah asks to die (1Ki 19:4) → "Arise and eat" (19:5, 7) → "in the strength of that food" to Horeb (19:8). Here the meal does not lower the guard. It carries an exhausted soul across from wanting to die to going on.
Life "better" gone: "take my life from me, for it is better for me to die" (Jon 4:3, 8); "take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers" (1Ki 19:4).
Face: S03 The soul dies, or asks to die; Hits: 15; Example: Num 23:10; Judg 16:30; Eze 18:4, 20; 1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:3, 8

The soul is said to die. "Let me die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his!" "Let me die with the Philistines." In both, the Hebrew is *let my soul die*. "Behold, all souls are mine … the soul who sins shall die." Elijah "asked that he might die" (literally, asked for his soul to die), and so did Jonah.
findings_in_focus.meaning: Meaning: *nephesh* ("soul, life") is used of the one who dies. It is not only something that leaves at death. Implies: Ch 2's "The soul departs" (Gen 35:18) is one face only. The same word is also the subject of dying.

findings_in_focus.text: R25 | Wanting to die | Of the wishes to die, four are answered with something other than death; three are granted | 1Ki 19:4–8; Jon 4:3, 9–11; Exo 16:3–4; Num 21:5–8; Judg 16:30; 9:54; 2Sa 1:9–16

It is built mostly from the M47 seat words (soul, spirit, breath, heart). M25's own roots appear only where those verses carry them: breathed: Gen 2:7; revived: Judg 15:19, Gen 45:27, 1Ki 17:22; die: 1Ki 19:4, Jon 4:3; death: Psa 116, 56:13; prolongs life: Pro 10:27

verses.text: When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, “ Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” And Elisha said, “ Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”

passage.text: Fifty men of the sons of the prophets also went and stood at some distance from them, as they both were standing by the Jordan.
Then Elijah took his cloak and rolled it up and struck the water, and the water was parted to the one side and to the other, till the two of them could go over on dry ground.
When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, “ Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” And Elisha said, “ Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me.”
And he said, “You have asked a hard thing; yet, if you see me as I am being taken from you, it shall be so for you, but if you do not see me, it shall not be so.”
And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.

findings_in_focus.text: 2Ki 2:2–6 | Elijah: "Please stay here" (three times) | Elisha: "As the Lord lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you" (three times) | "Let there be a double portion of your spirit on me" (2:9) → "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2:15; Batch F §9.5)

Asking for another's spirit: "'Ask what I shall do for you' … 'Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me'" (2Ki 2:9) [H2]. A human spirit is the object of petition, and it is transferable.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the outcome in context: the request is granted on condition of *seeing* Elijah taken (2:10); Elisha's first act is a question: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" (2:14); others then recognise it: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2:15); See Batch F §9.5.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Unclean spirits recognise the Son of God (Mar 3:11) and obey him (Mar 1:27).; Spirits either confess Jesus come in the flesh or are "the spirit of the antichrist" (1Jo 4:2–3).; They must be tested (1Jo 4:1), and the spirit of error stands against the Spirit of truth (1Jo 4:6).; The Lord can dispatch a lying spirit (1Ki 22:23). Ministering spirits serve (Heb 1:14).; Flesh in relating to God: "All flesh" is humanity as it comes to God: all flesh comes in prayer (Psa 65:2), sees salvation and glory (Luk 3:6; Isa 40:5), and blesses (Psa 145:21).; Covenant is cut in the flesh, and its inner counterpart is the circumcised heart (§7.2).; Flesh vs spirit as powers: Isa 31:3; Joh 6:63; 1Co 5:5; Jer 17:5.; The "life of the flesh is in the blood" (Lev 17:11) is the ground of atonement.; God is shown with his own heart and soul in these relations: his soul avenges (Jer 5:9) and he swears by it (Amo 6:8); he acts with all his heart and soul (Jer 32:41); he wishes for a heart in his people (Deu 5:29); his heart recoils in compassion (Hos 11:8); his soul delights in the servant (Isa 42:1); he gives up the beloved of his soul (Jer 12:7); the priest acts according to his heart and soul (1Sa 2:35); Speech and the heart. The heart speaks inwardly ("in the heart", §1.3), is spoken to ("to the heart" = comfort, §1.4), and its speech either matches the mouth or is betrayed by it. Hebrew prayer is an act of the heart that may or may not reach the lips.; Fringe worth keeping: *kāvôd* as the inner self (§3.2) — a possible inner-being term outside M47; the soul asked to die (§2); the double portion of another's spirit (2Ki 2:9); the dying soul naming a child and the returning spirit naming a spring (§1.8); Isaac's soul giving the blessing (§12); Qoheleth testing his own heart (Ecc 2:1); the Gentile's heart-and-conscience law-court (Rom 2:15); the flesh-then-breath sequence of the dry bones (Eze 37:6–8); "gain the whole world and forfeit his soul" (Mat 16:26); "transgression speaks [as an oracle] deep in his heart" (Psa 36:1); the heart with "highways to Zion" (Psa 84:5); "absent in body … present in spirit" (Col 2:5)
Revisit: Batch E §2 recorded 2Ki 2:9 only as "asking for another's spirit". Its outcome in 2:15 is part of the same relation.
Batch E v1 | §2 (2Ki 2:9), §7.1 (1Sa 18:3) | Pointers to F §9.5 (2Ki 2:9–15 outcome) and F §1.1 (Jonathan / Saul contrast) | Batch E v2
Shared between persons: souls knit, hearts joined or stolen, spirit passed on (1 Sam 18:1; 2 Sam 15:6; 2 Kgs 2:9).

3.8 The inner seat shared or joined between persons ◆ fringe cluster: *Soul to soul:*; "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (1Sa 18:1, 3; 20:17); "your friend who is as your own soul" (Deu 13:6, with "the wife you embrace"); "his life is bound up in the boy's life" (Gen 44:30); *Heart to heart:* "my heart will be joined to you" (1Ch 12:17); "Is your heart true to my heart as mine is to yours?" (2Ki 10:15); "you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together" (2Co 7:3); "I hold you in my heart" (Phili 1:7); "in person not in heart" (1Th 2:17).; *Shared across a group:* "one heart and soul" (Act 4:32); "one spirit, with one mind" (Phili 1:27); "Did we not act in the same spirit?" (2Co 12:18).; *Transferred between persons:* "a double portion of your spirit" (2Ki 2:9, 15); "take some of the Spirit that is on you and put it on them" (Num 11:17, 25); "in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children" (Luk 1:17; Mal 4:6).; *Captured or stolen by others:* "Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel" (2Sa 15:6); "his wives turned away his heart" (1Ki 11:3); "he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man" (2Sa 19:14).; *Known from shared experience:* "You know the heart [nephesh] of a sojourner, for you were sojourners" (Exo 23:9).; *With a spouse:* "guard yourselves in your spirit, and let none of you be faithless to the wife of your youth" (Mal 2:15–16); "one flesh" (Gen 2:24).; [Claude reading] The inner seat is not depicted as sealed inside the individual. It can be knit to, joined with, held within, carried in, stolen by, or shared with another person. It can also be passed from one person to another (spirit).

findings_in_focus.text: 9. Cross-cutting observations for Batch B [Claude reading]: The heart is the organ of attention, knowing, understanding, storing, remembering and reasoning. Attention is literally *setting the heart*. The heart's hardness is the same thing as failing to hear and understand.; The soul relates to knowledge by *receiving* it (pleasant, sweet, life-giving) and by dwelling on memories (bowed down). The soul can be commanded to remember. Soul-desire can run ahead of knowledge.; The human spirit is the seat of self-knowledge and searching. It knows a person's thoughts, makes understanding possible as God's breath in man, searches after the heart meditates, and perceives others' inner reasoning. A cool spirit (temper) is linked with understanding and restrained speech.; God's Spirit is the true source of knowledge, wisdom, skill, teaching, remembrance and prophecy. The heart or own spirit as a source of prophecy is condemned.; Hearing is the main channel into the inner seat. The ear receives; the heart keeps, understands or refuses. News makes hearts melt, spirits revive and souls refresh. God hears the heart. The "hearing heart" of 1 Kgs 3:9 is confirmed in the tags.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the context reads add two qualifications.; Hearing sometimes needs seeing. Jacob's spirit revives only when he sees the wagons (Gen 45:27, Batch G §2). Elisha receives the spirit on condition of seeing (2Ki 2:10, Batch F §9.5).; What is heard moves between people. Esau's heart-speech is reported (Gen 27:42, Batch F §8.2). A fainthearted soldier melts others (Deu 20:8, Batch F §6).; Word and breath belong together: creative word // breath of his mouth; Spirit and words in the mouth; empty words are "wind".; Flesh appears as a *way of knowing and judging* ("according to the flesh"), set against revelation from the Father and the Spirit.; Soul-ish vs spiritual (§8) is a genuine textual contrast between the soul and spirit orders, and it touches the open question from depiction v1.

2. Revival — the spirit returns: "Alive" runs through the scene: the son is alive (26, 28), the father's spirit comes alive (27), and the father now speaks of his own death (28).; As in 2Ki 2:10–15 (Batch F §9.5), seeing is the hinge.

Asking for another's spirit: "'Ask what I shall do for you' … 'Please let there be a double portion of your spirit on me'" (2Ki 2:9) [H2]. A human spirit is the object of petition, and it is transferable.; Revisit 2026-09-28: the outcome in context: the request is granted on condition of *seeing* Elijah taken (2:10); Elisha's first act is a question: "Where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?" (2:14); others then recognise it: "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2:15); See Batch F §9.5.

verses.text: But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.”

passage.text: Again the Lord spoke to Ahaz:
“ Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven.”
But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test.”
And he said, “ Hear then, O house of David! Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.

findings_in_focus.text: Led to: Ahaz refuses the sign the Lord offers: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). So *"the Lord himself will give you a sign … Immanuel"* (v14).

Isaiah 43:10: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand": The setting is a court. The nations are summoned: *"All the nations gather together … Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right"* (v9). Israel is brought out as the Lord's witness, and described as unfit for it: *"Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears!"* (v8).; Then: *"You are my witnesses," declares the Lord, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (v10). The knowing, believing and understanding are the purpose of the choosing. They are not its ground. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen. They were chosen in order to come to know.; This is the reverse of the order in §2a, where the child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). There the knowing comes before the person's own choosing. Here, the knowing follows God's choosing of the person. Each verse states its own order.; What the chosen are to know is one thing: *"that I am he. Before me no god was formed"* (v10). The Lord's own witness follows: *"I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you"* (v12).; The oracles that follow set the chosen beside those who make idols: The chosen people do not perceive what God is doing: *"Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?"* (43:19). "Perceive" is the same word as "know" in v10 (H3045).; The idol-makers' witnesses *"neither see nor know"* (44:9).; Of the idol-maker himself: *"They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand"* (44:18). "Know" and "discern" are the same words as "know" and "understand" in 43:10 (H3045, H0995).; The chosen people are also accused: *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (43:22); *"you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities"* (43:24). Then comes the answer: *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (43:25).

Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

Choosing has two sides: Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.; Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.; The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

findings_in_focus.text: No other M-code characteristic co-occurs in this verse alongside the seeking of the priesthood.

God is the initiator here ('by those who did not seek me' being sought BY God), an inversion where God is subject seeking out a nation that itself did not seek him -- the direction is God toward the unresponsive nation.

M42 (called, H7121H) co-occurs describing the nation not being 'called by God's name'; it characterizes the unresponsive nation's identity, distinct from the inquiring/seeking dynamic itself which here is enacted by God, not the nation.

In Isa.65.1 God's readiness to be sought by those who did not ask reveals his own disposition/perception that he is available and near even to those not yet oriented toward him -- a divine self-disclosure of gracious accessibility rather than a human perception.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

God's extension of the characteristic -- his readiness to be sought even by those who did not ask (Isa.65.1) and his invitation 'Seek me and live' (Amos.5.4) -- shows a disposition of gracious accessibility and desire for relationship with humanity, contrasted with his refusal to be inquired of by the unrepentant and idolatrous (Ezek.20.3, 20.31), revealing a disposition that is both inviting and holy/discerning.

Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in": This is an oracle. It opens with God, not with the people: *"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me … I said, “Here I am, here I am,”"* (v1); *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices"* (v2); The wrong choosing in v12 is made in front of a God who is calling and holding out his hands.; The oracle shows what they turned to instead: sacrifices *"in gardens"*, sitting *"in tombs"*, eating *"pig’s flesh"* (v3–4); a pride that says *"do not come near me, for I am too holy for you"* (v5); they *"forget my holy mountain"* and *"set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny"* (v11); They put their trust in luck and fate.; The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.; The verse then gives the reason, and the reason is in the inner being: *"because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."* The choosing does not stand alone. It is the far end of not answering and not listening. When they turned away from the voice calling them, that was already a choice, and choosing what God does not delight in is where it ends.; There is a phrase to set beside Joshua 24. There, the choice turned on what was *"evil in your eyes"*. Here they *"did what was evil in my eyes"*. The measure has moved from their eyes to God's, and his delight is the standard their choice is judged by.; In the same oracle the word "chosen" is used of the others: *"my chosen shall possess it"* (v9); *"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse"* (v15); So in one passage there are those who chose what God did not delight in, and those God calls *"my chosen"*. The outcome sets the two side by side and reaches the inner being on both sides: *"my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (v14). The choice ends in the heart and spirit of the one who made it.

Choosing before a God who has already acted: In these verses the human choice is never the first move.; At Shechem it comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning with *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Jos 24:3).; In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2).; At the Jerusalem council the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Act 15:7), in the same verb.

13. Cross-cutting observations for Batch E [Claude reading]: Relating to God engages the whole inner seat, and the texts say so by formula.; "With all your heart and with all your soul" governs: serving (Deu 10:12; Jos 22:5); keeping the law and renewing the covenant (2Ki 23:3; 2Ch 34:31; Deu 30:10); loving after circumcision of heart (Deu 30:6); praying and returning (1Ki 8:48); being tested (Deu 13:3); "With my whole heart" governs thanks, praise, crying and seeking.; The formula also appears of God (Jer 32:41).; The heart is where the relation to God is located, examined and known.; It prays without voice (1Sa 1:13) and cries (Lam 2:18).; It holds the law (Psa 37:31) and trusts (Psa 28:7).; It believes (Rom 10:10) and is circumcised (Deu 30:6).; It is the organ God tests (§8.1). Knowing hearts is the ground of God's forgiveness (1Ki 8:39) and of his giving the Spirit (Act 15:8).; Where heart and lips diverge, the lips do not count (Hos 7:14; Isa 29:13).; The soul is the self in address. It is spoken to by its owner ("Bless the Lord, O my soul"; "Why are you cast down, O my soul"), and asked to be spoken to by God ("Say to my soul, 'I am your salvation'", Psa 35:3). It is also the life that is: asked for (Est 7:3; 1Ki 17:21); asked to die (1Ki 19:4; Jon 4:8); redeemed, ransomed and atoned for (§9.1, §11.1); delivered or lost (§11.3); The human spirit is most active in this batch.; It prays and sings apart from the mind (1Co 14:14–16).; It serves (Rom 1:9) and worships in spirit (Joh 4:23–24).; It rejoices in the Savior (Luk 1:47) and is renewed (Eze 36:26; Eph 4:23).; It receives the benediction "grace be with your spirit".; At death it is the part committed to God (Psa 31:5; Luk 23:46; Act 7:59; Mat 27:50).; Its complaint voices anguish (Job 7:11), and its brokenness blocks hearing (Exo 6:9).; The divine Spirit relates to God on the person's behalf.; It cries "Abba" in the heart (Gal 4:6) and intercedes within the searched heart (Rom 8:26–27).; It bears witness (Heb 10:15) and writes on hearts (2Co 3:3).; It circumcises the heart (Rom 2:29) and renews (Tit 3:5).; It gives faith and gifts (1Co 12:9; Gal 3:2) and speaks through the prophet (2Sa 23:2).; It can itself be tested (Act 5:9), resisted (Act 7:51) and outraged (Heb 10:29).; Other spirits relate to God too, and are judged by that relation.
