findings_in_focus.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

findings_in_focus.text: In 1 Chr 10:13 darash ('seeking guidance') again sits within the base sense of consulting a medium, paralleling Deut 18:11's usage with no additional divergence.

M57 (breach of faith, H4603/H4604) and M65 (command, H1697G) are present in 1 Chr 10:13 alongside the seeking; the seeking-of-a-medium is presented as the culminating instance/proof of the breach of faith and failure to keep the command -- the seeking characteristic supplies the concrete act that instantiates the abstract unfaithfulness named by the other M-codes.

In 1 Chr 10:13 the operation 'died' (H4191, role-T3) applies to Saul; the seeking (H1875, consulting the medium) is Saul's own initiating act directed toward the medium as the consulted party, which precipitates the death operation upon himself.

The 'inquired'/'seeking'/'searched' occurrences in this pass show the root's outer boundary away from formal cultic consultation: Lev.10.16 (procedural cultic checking of a sacrifice), 2Sam.11.3 (mundane social inquiry about a woman's identity), Jer.38.4/2Chr.31.21 (civic/devotional 'seeking welfare' or 'seeking God' as ongoing disposition), Ps.109.10 (destitute foraging for food), Ezek.34.8 (pastoral searching for lost sheep), and Judg.6.29 (forensic investigation of who committed a deed) -- these occurrences share the base sense of careful, purposeful inquiry but apply it to secular, pastoral, or forensic objects rather than deity/oracle consultation, showing the root's flexibility extends the subgroup's core 'formal consultation' sense outward to any object warranting diligent investigation.

Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good": The setting is a king’s heart in fear. Syria and Ephraim are marching on Jerusalem, and *"the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind"* (v2). The Lord sends Isaiah with a word for that heart: *"Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint"* (v4); the threat *"shall not stand"* (v7); then the condition: *"If you are not firm in faith, you will not be firm at all"* (v9). Both "firm" words are the one verb (H0539), so standing firm and being kept firm are the same word.; Then the Lord makes Ahaz an offer: *"Ask a sign of the Lord your God; let it be deep as Sheol or high as heaven"* (v11). Ahaz refuses, in pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (v12). The answer shows what that refusal was: *"Is it too little for you to weary men, that you weary my God also?"* (v13). Ahaz’s refusal was a choice. He chose not to take hold of what the Lord held out.; The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides: refusing the evil (H3988A); choosing the good (H0977); Refusing is not a step before the choice. It is the choice seen from the other side. Both rest on a knowing: *"when he knows how"*. The verse marks the moment a person can tell evil from good and turn from the one to the other.; The verse ties the eating to that knowing: he eats *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The oracle itself says what curds and honey are. *"In that day … because of the abundance of milk that they give, he will eat curds, for everyone who is left in the land will eat curds and honey"* (v21–22). It is the food of those left in the land after the Lord has swept it with *"the king of Assyria"*: vineyards turned to *"briers and thorns"*, hills *"where cattle are let loose"* (v23–25). The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats with those who are left, and eats from abundance, in a land stripped of what it had.

findings_in_focus.text: Factor Joined with: Confirmed. grief (Mar 3:5); jealousy, which makes it unappeasable (Pro 6:34; 27:4); envy (Gal 5:26; Jam 4:2); the Spirit (1Sa 11:6).
Sequence in Jam 4:1–3: passions at war within → desire unmet → murder, covet → fight and quarrel → not asking → asking wrongly.

Anger and Desire, jealousy, envy (M18): Jealousy named with God's anger; "jealousy makes a man furious"; "the anger and envy that you showed because of your hatred"; "You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel".

passions at war within → quarrels and fights (Jam 4:1); covet, cannot obtain → fight and quarrel (4:2); jealousy and strife → of the flesh (1Cor 3:3); conceit, craving → quarrels about words → envy, dissension, slander (1Ti 6:4); controversies → breed quarrels (2Ti 2:23).

Where it comes from. Every verse, or the one next to it, names a source, and the sources are inner: Passions at war within: "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (Jam 4:1–2). The outer fight is the inner war carried outward; The flesh: "for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1Cor 3:3), after "I could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh" (3:1); Conceit: "Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another" (Gal 5:26). "He is puffed up with conceit and understands nothing. He has an unhealthy craving for controversy" (1Ti 6:4); Appetite: the dividers "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites [belly]" (Rom 16:18); Envy and selfish ambition behind a good act: "Some indeed preach Christ from envy and rivalry, but others from good will … The former proclaim Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely but thinking to afflict me" (Phili 1:15–17). The same outward act, preaching, has opposite inner sources; A depraved mind: "constant friction among people who are depraved in mind and deprived of the truth, imagining that godliness is a means of gain" (1Ti 6:5); Controversies themselves: "foolish, ignorant controversies … breed quarrels" (2Ti 2:23); "avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law" (Tit 3:9).

How it co-exists: With envy, often (5 of the 11 verses). Envy is paired with strife in Gal 5:26; Phili 1:15; 1Ti 6:4; 1Cor 3:3 ("jealousy"); in Jam 4:2 it is "covet"; With its named opposites: "that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment" (1Cor 1:10); "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6); "the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone … correcting his opponents with gentleness" (2Ti 2:24–25); "keep in step with the Spirit" (Gal 5:25).

What it leads to. Separation from the divider: "avoid them" (Rom 16:17); "after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him … he is self-condemned" (Tit 3:10–11). "You do not have, because you do not ask" (Jam 4:2), so strife blocks asking.

I read: the delight is real enough to be named, but it is delight in what they have not yet faced. 10.7 *Others around a choice*: Mal 3:1–2 beside Isa 58:2

An inner act weighed by what God chooses: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).; The self-humbling they offered was not wrong in itself. The passage says it stood beside oppression and quarrelling in the same people, and that it was not what he chooses.

findings_in_focus.text: Inside one person, perception is blocked, then fear, then rivalry (Luk 9:45-46).

What it leads to, in the person. Fear to ask (Luk 9:45); a plea, "I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me!" (Psa 119:19); searching, "the glory of kings is to search things out" (Pro 25:2); obedience to what is revealed, "the things that are revealed belong to us … that we may do all the words of this law" (Deu 29:29). Job 3:23, "a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in", is the not-knowing that hems in.

Seat.; In the verse: none of the 13 names a seat.; In the passage — new in v3: in six passages the seat arrives close by. Each time it is genuine, but it belongs to a different party or plays a different role: The other party names it. Luk 9:45–46 → 9:47 "But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child". The disciples' blocked perception, their fear of asking and their rivalry have no seat word. The seat appears only when Jesus reads it: their hearts, known by another. This matches what v1 §3 item 1 found for doubt (Luk 24:38): the seat is named when someone diagnoses.; The offender's heart as the cause. Isa 29:14 ← 29:13 "their hearts are far from me" (v2; Batch G v3 §12.3). Hidden discernment is the consequence of a heart that has gone elsewhere.; The bearer's own heart as the prayer's end. Psa 19:12 (hidden faults) → 19:14 "Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight". The one who cannot see his own hidden faults hands the heart's meditation over to God's sight. What is hidden from the self is entrusted to the one from whom nothing is hidden (§6).; The bearer's own soul as the source of the plea. Psa 119:19 ("hide not your commandments from me!") → 119:20 "My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times". The plea not to have the commandments hidden comes from a soul consumed with longing for them. Here the not-knowing is feared, and the fear comes from desire, the reverse of Luk 9:45, where the disciples are afraid to ask.; Heart and soul in the response to what is revealed. Deu 29:29 → 30:2 "return to the Lord your God … and obey his voice … with all your heart and with all your soul". The revealed things (29:29) are to be done, and the next verses place that doing in the whole heart and soul.; The sufferer's soul. Job 3:23 ("a man whose way is hidden") sits in the passage opened by "life to the bitter in soul" (3:20; see §4). The hemmed-in man is the bitter soul.

findings_in_focus.text: In Esth.6.2, Job.10.6, Ps.24.6, Ps.27.4, Ps.34.14, Ps.35.4, and Ps.37.36 baqash is used in its standard senses (hostile pursuit, investigative search, devotional seeking, seeking peace) with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

Other M-codes present in Ps.27.4: M21 (asked), M18 (beauty). Baqash (seek) here names the psalmist's total posture toward the Lord's house, which is expressed concretely through asking (M21) and gazing on beauty (M18); baqash functions as the umbrella intention, not a modifier of either.

In Ps.27.4, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by the psalmist, directed toward the Lord — specifically toward dwelling in his house and gazing on his beauty, marking God as the object of pursuit.

findings_in_focus.text: Deuteronomy 12:18: "And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake": The chapter opens by clearing away the places of the nations: *"You shall surely destroy all the places where the nations whom you shall dispossess served their gods"* (v2). Then: *"You shall not worship the Lord your God in that way. But you shall seek the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (v4–5). Two measures are set against each other: *"You shall not do according to all that we are doing here today, everyone doing whatever is right in his own eyes"* (v8). The place God chooses replaces the places a person sees for himself: *"Take care that you do not offer your burnt offerings at any place that you see, but at the place that the Lord will choose"* (v13–14).; Rejoicing is commanded three times in the chapter, each time at the chosen place and *"before the Lord"*: *"there you shall eat before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your households, in all that you undertake, in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (v7); *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your sons and your daughters, your male servants and your female servants, and the Levite that is within your towns, since he has no portion or inheritance with you"* (v12); *"you shall eat them before the Lord your God in the place that the Lord your God will choose, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite … And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (v18); The ground of the joy is named in v7: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"*. The place is where the joy is had. The blessing is what it is about.; The joy is not had alone. The household, the servants and the Levite are named in it each time. The verse after v18 turns the same thought into a warning: *"Take care that you do not neglect the Levite as long as you live in your land"* (v19).

Morphologically, both H0149 and H0629 are invariant adverbs (AD) across every occurrence in this subgroup -- there is no stem/voice variation to check for meaning-relevance in either term; both are fixed adverbial intensifiers with no active/passive/causative distinction possible, a genuine no-distinction-found result for the morph-reading requirement.

The immediate response denoted (complete, prompt execution of a command) is consistent across every occurrence of both strongs -- payment 'in full without delay' (6.8), decree carried out 'with all diligence' (6.12, 7.21, 6.13), building progressing 'diligently' (5.8), purchase/offering 'with all diligence' (7.17), judgment executed 'strictly' (7.26), and compliance 'in full' (7.23) all show the same uniform thoroughness-response, varying only in the domain of the act, not in the quality of response.

No movement across constitutional levels or from an external spirit is shown -- the characteristic moves entirely at the level of external administrative behavior, originating from a decree (spoken/written command) and terminating in an external act of compliance, with no mention of internal transmission through spirit, soul, or body. No prior reception or becoming is described before a person extends the characteristic -- treasurers and governors are simply commanded by decree to comply; there is no narrated transformation or endowment that precedes their giving.

The characteristic consistently co-occurs with decree/authority vocabulary (H4430 king, H5648 done/executed) and with terms for royal or divine wrath/judgment (H7109 wrath in 7.23; judicial penalty terms in 7.26) -- these adjacent characteristics of authority and consequence appear in nearly every occurrence, showing the diligence-term is never isolated but always framed by a command-and-consequence structure.

The characteristic consistently follows a decree/command in sequence -- in every occurrence a decree is issued first ('I make a decree...', 'whatever is decreed...') and the diligence/fullness term describes the response that follows; the sequence is always command-then-compliance, never the reverse.

The characteristic is produced by an issued decree/command -- it does not arise spontaneously but is generated as the required response to an authoritative order (royal decree in 6.12/6.13/7.21/7.26; divine decree in 7.17/7.23).

findings_in_focus.text: Part 2 verses: what they add. The four strands hold, and each gains an instance: Strand (a), a demand no one can meet, with the angry one now the demander. "There is not a man on earth who can meet the king's demand … no one can show it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh" (Dan 2:10–11). Then "Because of this the king was angry and very furious, and commanded that all the wise men of Babylon be destroyed" (2:12). This is the mirror of Gen 30:2. Jacob, faced with an impossible demand, named God as the only one who could meet it. Nebuchadnezzar hears the same answer ("except the gods") and orders a massacre; The anger is answered by "prudence and discretion" (Dan 2:14): Daniel's; Strand (b), thwarted and made a fool of. "Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children" (Mat 2:16). "Tricked" is Balaam's "you have made a fool of me" (Num 22:29). This time the killing is carried out, and it ends in "Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted" (Mat 2:18); Strand (d), refused by subordinates; Nebuchadnezzar "in furious rage" at the three who "do not serve your gods" (Dan 3:12–13); After their answer, "But if not … we will not serve your gods" (3:18), "Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more" (3:19); The face changes outward, against them. This is the reverse of §1's fallen face, which turns inward; The outcome reverses the anger: "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego … who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command" (3:28). The king blesses the very refusal that enraged him; A new instance, thwarted from outside and turned against the weaker: "ships of Kittim shall come against him, and he shall be afraid and withdraw, and shall turn back and be enraged and take action against the holy covenant" (Dan 11:30). "News from the east and the north shall alarm him, and he shall go out with great fury to destroy" (11:44). Fear comes first, then anger. The anger is turned on a weaker target than the one that thwarted him.

Seat . No in-verse seat in the six: Outside the verse: Dan 11:28 "his heart shall be set against the holy covenant". Genuine. The bearer's own, two verses before the rage. The heart was set before the thwarting. The anger only releases it; Dan 2:11 "not with flesh". Spurious as a seat: flesh as the human realm.

G0154 aiteo, 'asks': to request something from another. In this passage it is the request of a petitioner to a giver, as in 7:9 'if his son asks him for bread'.
'everyone' makes the statement of 7:8 hold for each asker: no person or condition is named that would exclude any.
G3956 pas, 'everyone': each one, all; here in the nominative with the participle 'who asks'.
'receives' is what asking yields in 7:8: the asker takes what is given. The verse does not name the giver.
G2983 lambano, 'receives': to take or get; here to get what was asked, answering 7:7 'it will be given to you'.
In 7:8 'seeks' is the second act of the series and is answered by 'finds'; the verse does not name what is sought.
G2212 zeteo, 'seeks': to look for, to search for something. Here it is the seeker's own pursuit, answered by finding.
'finds' is what seeking yields in 7:8: the seeker comes upon what was sought.
G2147 heurisko, 'finds': to find, to come upon what was looked for.
'knocks' is the third act of the series in 7:8 and is answered by 'opened'; the verse does not say at what, or who answers.
G2925 krouo, 'knocks': to strike, as at a door to be let in.
'it will be opened' is a passive: the opening is done by one the verse does not name, and it answers the knocking.
G0455 anoigo, 'opened': to open; in the passive, to be opened, here to the one who knocks.

What the three answers give the three acts in Mat 7:8: 'receives' gives asking its result of being given, 'finds' gives seeking its result of coming upon, 'opened' gives knocking its result of being let in; each act has its own answer.
'For' in Mat 7:8 gives the ground of the commands of 7:7: it says why asking, seeking and knocking are to be done. It has no inner-being bearing of its own.
The two 'and' in Mat 7:8 join the three clauses of asking, seeking and knocking; they have no inner-being bearing of their own.
'Hear' is an imperative from Job to the Lord: Job asks to be heard before he speaks.
H8085 shama, 'hear': to hear, to listen; in the imperative, a call to attend to what follows.
'I will speak' is Job's stated intention, in the imperfect, first person: he will speak after he has been heard.
H1696 dabar, 'speak': to speak, to say; here Job's own speech, set beside his questioning.

'I will question you' is Job's act toward the Lord, in the imperfect, first person: he takes the part of questioner, and the one questioned is God. The same words stand in Job 38:3 and Job 40:7, where the Lord speaks them to Job.
H7592 sha'al, 'question': to ask, to inquire; here to put questions to another for an answer, which the second half of the verse names ('you make it known to me').
'you make it known to me' is Job's request of the Lord, in the causative stem: the knowing is to come from the one questioned.
H3045 yada, 'known': to know; in the causative stem, to make known, to let someone know.
What 'you make it known to me' gives the questioning in Job 42:4: it names the end of the question, which is that the one questioned makes known to the questioner.
The conjunction prefixed to 'speak' in Job 42:4 joins 'Hear' to 'I will speak'; it has no inner-being bearing of its own.
'He inquired about their welfare' is Joseph's own act toward his brothers, in the narrative past. What he asks about is named at once: their welfare, then his father.
H7592 sha'al, 'inquired': to ask, to inquire; with 'welfare' as its object, it is asking after another's state, a greeting of inquiry.
'welfare' is the thing inquired about: the brothers' state of peace or well-being, asked of them by Joseph.
H7965 shalom, 'welfare': peace, well-being; here the condition of persons asked after.
'said' opens Joseph's spoken questions after the narrated inquiry.
H0559 amar, 'said': to say; here introducing the words of the question.
'father' is the one Joseph asks about, named to the brothers as 'your father'.
H0001 ab, 'father': a father; here the person the question is about.
'well' in 'Is your father well' is the same word as 'welfare' in the first clause: the question puts the earlier inquiry to the father's case.
H7965 shalom, 'well': peace, well-being; in 'Is your father well' it asks whether he is in good state.
'the old man' is a second name for the father, set after 'your father'.
H2205 zaqen, 'old man': aged, elder; here the father as aged.
'of whom you spoke' recalls what the brothers had said to Joseph earlier; the question rests on their own speech.
H0559 amar, 'spoke': to say; here the brothers' earlier statement about their father.
The relative 'whom' in Gen 43:27 ties the old man to the brothers' earlier words; it has no inner-being bearing of its own.
'Is he still alive?' asks whether the father lives; it is Joseph's second question, after 'Is your father well', and the brothers answer it in 43:28 with 'he is still alive'.
H2416 chay, 'alive': living; here the state asked about, whether the father is yet living.
'still' in 'still alive' asks whether the father lives yet, after the time that has passed.
H5750 od, 'still': yet, again; here with 'alive': 'Is he still alive?'.
